title: "Laboratories"

A laboratory on this site is a figure with the population known, so the error is visible. The controls change one piece of a model. Where a formula exists, the figure uses it. A simulation or a normal approximation is labelled as one.

The kernel density page came first. The other three are the same idea for a prior, a transition matrix, and a confidence interval.

## Kernel density

A Gaussian kernel turns a sample into a density. The bandwidth $h$ is the choice. A small $h$ leaves a bump on the observations: high variance, low bias. A large $h$ washes the modes out. The page keeps the sample still and moves $h$, and it plots that sample's integrated squared error against the mean integrated squared error of a sample of the same size. The estimate does not use the true density. Both errors do.

[Open the kernel density laboratory](kernel-density.qmd).

## Beta–Binomial updating

A coin has unknown heads probability $\theta$, and the prior is a Beta distribution. After $x$ heads in $n$ tosses the posterior is $\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha+x,\beta+n-x)$. The posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean and $x/n$, with weight $(\alpha+\beta)/(\alpha+\beta+n)$ on the prior. Future tosses are predicted by the beta–binomial average over that posterior, which is wider than a binomial that fixes $\theta$ at the posterior mean.

[Open the Beta–Binomial laboratory](beta-binomial.qmd).

## A Markov chain

On a finite set of states the whole process is a transition matrix $P$. From a chosen start, the distribution after $t$ steps is the corresponding row of $P^{t}$. A stationary distribution satisfies $\pi=\pi P$. When the chain is one closed aperiodic class, every start forgets itself and $P^{t}$ settles on $\pi$. A periodic chain can have a stationary distribution while $P^{t}$ keeps oscillating. Two closed classes mean two stationary distributions, and one path's time average follows the class the path happens to enter.

[Open the Markov chain laboratory](markov-chain.qmd).

## Coverage of a confidence interval

The confidence is the probability, before the sample is drawn, that the random interval contains the parameter. This page draws the interval repeatedly from a known population and marks the misses. For a normal sample the $t$ interval hits with probability exactly equal to the stated level. Using a normal quantile with the sample standard deviation $s$ hits less often. For a proportion, the exact coverage of the Wald and Wilson intervals is a sum over the binomial distribution, and Wald's sum falls away from the stated level when the probability is near $0$ or $1$.

[Open the confidence interval laboratory](ci-coverage.qmd).
